text.text: Moreover, this WEIRD bias was particularly concentrated in the United States and other English-speaking developed countries, rather than being evenly distributed across Western societies.

text.text: Eight percent of articles used representative samples, with a bias in favor of female participants in non-representative samples-especially in feminism, where 78% of participants were female.
The dominance of samples composed of students is in line with the historical development of psychological research (Henrich et al., 2010).

text.text: In our reviewed articles, it was not until 2015 that student samples were surpassed by non-representative samples from the general population.
Nevertheless, students remained the second most common type of sample until the end of the historical series, especially considering that a substantial number of mixed samples also included students.
Samples focused on specific populations (e.g., activists, members of associations, etc.) have also been more numerous than representative samples.

Student samples are frequently used across nearly all ideologies, while general population samples are particularly prominent in the study of left-wing authoritarianism, left-wing political orientation, and operational left-wing ideology.
As can be seen from Figure 3, psychometric tools for each left-wing ideology exhibit distinct usage patterns.
text.formatted: As can be seen from Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>, psychometric tools for each left-wing ideology exhibit distinct usage patterns.

text.text: Measures of political orientation have increased sharply since the early 2000s, reflecting an emphasis on general political identity.

As shown in Table 1, 51% of the articles reported measures of political orientation, of which 93% were single items, mostly bipolar (i.e., a Likert scale ranging from left/liberal to right/conservative).
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, 51% of the articles reported measures of political orientation, of which 93% were single items, mostly bipolar (i.e., a Likert scale ranging from left/liberal to right/conservative).

text.text: These measures dominate the current landscape, yet they are far from standardized and exhibit substantial variability in format.
Of 1,021 samples in which a single-item political orientation scale was used, 14 did not report their response formats.
Among the 1,007 that did, 7-point scales were the most common (529 samples, 52.53%), followed by 5-point (183, 18.17%), 9-point (75, 7.45%), 11-point (66, 6.55%), and 10-point scales (45, 4.47%).
The remaining 109 samples (10.82%) used a variety of formats with up to 201 response options (Table S2).
text.formatted: The remaining 109 samples (10.82%) used a variety of formats with up to 201 response options (Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Measures of feminism were present in 31% of the reviewed articles.
This construct was most frequently measured between the late 1970s and the 1990s, followed by a decline that extended from around 2008 to 2019.
Environmentalism and operational left-wing ideology, both present in 13% of the articles, show a steady increase from around 2009.
More recently, new measurement models for progressivism and left-wing authoritarianism have emerged, while communism and egalitarianism present long but sporadic and low-frequency trajectories.
Together, these four ideologies exhibit low prevalence, below 3% of the reviewed articles.
The temporal trend of each category in articles reusing macro-survey data can be seen in Figure S2.
text.formatted: The temporal trend of each category in articles reusing macro-survey data can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S2</ref>.

text.text: These start from the 1980s and the single-item political orientation scale is also the dominant measure, followed by operational ideology and environmentalism.
We did not find measurements of left-wing authoritarianism or progressivism in these macro surveys.
Note.
Psychometric refinement is defined as either the shortening, translation, or adaptation of an existing measure.
Table S1 contains an equivalent, although more limited, account of information regarding articles reusing data from macro-surveys.

text.text: Psychometric characteristics reported in the reviewed articles varied across ideological constructs, both in terms of measurement strategies and the reporting of validation procedures.
Single-item scales were used in 53% of articles and were especially prevalent in studies that measured political orientation (93%).
Multi-item instruments appeared in 57% of articles, with particularly high proportions in studies on feminism (88%), egalitarianism (88%), communism (68%), and left-wing authoritarianism (100%).
Despite extensive use of multi-item instruments, only 2% of articles reported original validation procedures.

Psychometric refinements-defined as the shortening, translation, or adaptation of existing measures-were reported in 6% of articles and were more frequent in research on feminism (11%) and environmentalism (12%).
As shown in Figure 4, studies reporting either original validation or psychometric refinement increased notably from 2010.
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>, studies reporting either original validation or psychometric refinement increased notably from 2010.

text.text: Reporting factor analyses was relatively infrequent (8%), though more common in environmentalism (22%) and feminism (11%).
Internal consistency was reported in 31% of studies, with the highest proportions in environmentalism (67%), left-wing authoritarianism (92%), feminism (41%), and operational ideology (45%).

Reuse of existing instruments was observed in 62% of studies, particularly in feminism (72%), environmentalism (62%), and communism (68%), while the use of ad-hoc measures was reported in 25% of articles, with higher proportions in operational ideology (40%) and egalitarianism (48%).
As shown in Figure 4, while the reuse of existing measures has increased steadily since the late 1990s, the use of ad-hoc instruments has also grown in parallel.
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>, while the reuse of existing measures has increased steadily since the late 1990s, the use of ad-hoc instruments has also grown in parallel.

text.text: The relatively low overall prevalence of psychometric analyses should be interpreted in light of the frequent reuse of established measures, for which repeating psychometric assessments in every study would not necessarily be expected.

However, limited psychometric reporting was also evident among newly constructed measures: among articles employing multi-item ad hoc scales, 43% did not report an estimate of internal consistency, 83% did not report a factor analysis, and 38% reported neither.

These results indicate that, while some ideological domains have been measured with relatively greater attention to psychometric detail (i.e., environmentalism and feminism), reporting of internal consistency and factorial structure remains limited.
As can be seen from Figure 5, the single-item left-right scale measuring political orientation has dominated the field over the last two decades.
text.formatted: As can be seen from Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref>, the single-item left-right scale measuring political orientation has dominated the field over the last two decades.

text.text: However, in recent years, a growing number of studies have adopted approaches asking differentiated single-item questions for general, social, and economic political orientation.
Figure 5 also shows that measurement of feminism has shifted considerably.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref> also shows that measurement of feminism has shifted considerably.

text.text: Instruments such as the Attitudes Toward Women Scale (Spence & Helmreich, 1972) have declined in use, replaced by self-identification scales and multifactorial models like the Feminist Identity Development Scale (FIDS; Bargad & Hyde, 1991).
text.formatted: Instruments such as the Attitudes Toward Women Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Spence & Helmreich, 1972)</ref> have declined in use, replaced by self-identification scales and multifactorial models like the Feminist Identity Development Scale (FIDS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bargad & Hyde, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: These newer instruments often focus more on identity, general attitudes toward feminism or steps of identification with the feminist movement rather than on specific ideological content.
Notably, the Feminist Perspectives Scale (FPS) includes theoretically grounded subscales representing distinct strands of feminist theory (Henley et al., 1998; Henley et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Notably, the Feminist Perspectives Scale (FPS) includes theoretically grounded subscales representing distinct strands of feminist theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Henley et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Henley et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: However, the FPS remains underutilized in research and, therefore, is not visible in the most frequent measurement models displayed in Figure 5.
text.formatted: However, the FPS remains underutilized in research and, therefore, is not visible in the most frequent measurement models displayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref>.

text.text: Regarding environmentalism, the New Environmental Paradigm (NEP) scale has historically been the dominant instrument for assessing environmentalism (Dunlap, 2008; Dunlap & Mertig, 1992).
text.formatted: Regarding environmentalism, the New Environmental Paradigm (NEP) scale has historically been the dominant instrument for assessing environmentalism <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Dunlap, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Dunlap & Mertig, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: However, recent years have seen a diversification in measurement strategies, with increasing reliance on broader and often less psychometrically established scales assessing general environmental concern and measures of identification and engagement with the environmental movement.

These instruments vary widely in content and lack consistent factorial structures, echoing a broader trend toward measuring diffuse concerns and attitudes rather than specific theoretical frameworks or ideological commitments.

This systematic review identified only two studies that examined progressivism as a psychological construct, employing the Social Justice Scale (Torres-Harding et al., 2012) and the Progressive Values Scale (Proulx et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This systematic review identified only two studies that examined progressivism as a psychological construct, employing the Social Justice Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Torres-Harding et al., 2012)</ref> and the Progressive Values Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Proulx et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The Social Justice Scale represents a more general attempt to assess engagement with social justice causes and values, emphasizing activism and perceived importance of social justice in everyday life.
In contrast, the Progressive Values Scale offers an ideological model targeting core principles of what is referred to-often pejorativelyas "woke ideology" (Pluckrose & Lindsay, 2020).
text.formatted: In contrast, the Progressive Values Scale offers an ideological model targeting core principles of what is referred to-often pejorativelyas "woke ideology" <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Pluckrose & Lindsay, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It includes items tapping into mandated diversity, cultural appropriation, systemic oppression, and public censure.
While both instruments represent promising steps toward operationalizing progressive ideology, their empirical application remains scarce.
Measurement of operational left-wing ideology is characterized by highly heterogeneous instruments.

Although some established scales exist-notably the IPIP Liberalism/Conservatism Scale (Goldberg et al., 2006) and the Wilson-Patterson scale (Wilson & Patterson, 1968)-the field largely relies on diverse issue-based items that vary widely across studies.
text.formatted: Although some established scales exist-notably the IPIP Liberalism/Conservatism Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Goldberg et al., 2006)</ref> and the Wilson-Patterson scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Wilson & Patterson, 1968</ref>)-the field largely relies on diverse issue-based items that vary widely across studies.

text.text: These often combine attitudes toward social and economic matters without being grounded in a specific theoretical framework or showing a clear factorial structure.

At the same time, some degree of heterogeneity is difficult to avoid, because the political issues that meaningfully distinguish ideological positions vary across historical periods and sociopolitical contexts, requiring researchers to make context-sensitive decisions about item content.

In this regard, research shows that even validated instruments, like the Wilson-Patterson scale, are applied inconsistently across studies-varying in the number of items used, scale formats, and scoring methods-undermining consistency and generalizability (Azevedo & Bolesta, 2021).
text.formatted: In this regard, research shows that even validated instruments, like the Wilson-Patterson scale, are applied inconsistently across studies-varying in the number of items used, scale formats, and scoring methods-undermining consistency and generalizability <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Azevedo & Bolesta, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our results reflect this fragmentation, revealing that operational left-wing ideology lacks psychometrically robust and theoretically integrated measurement models.
Egalitarianism also lacks established measurement models.
Aside from ad hoc measures, the Humanism-Egalitarianism Scale (Katz & Hass, 1988) was employed in only two studies, strongly limiting the comparability of egalitarianism-related research.
text.formatted: Aside from ad hoc measures, the Humanism-Egalitarianism Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Katz & Hass, 1988</ref>) was employed in only two studies, strongly limiting the comparability of egalitarianism-related research.

text.text: Similarly, no stable measurement models exist for endorsement of communism as an ideology.

Early scholarly interest led to the development of the Attitudes Toward Communism Scale in the 1930s and 1940s, but no remarkable psychometric developments occurred until the introduction of the Belief in Communism Scale (McFarland, 1998).
text.formatted: Early scholarly interest led to the development of the Attitudes Toward Communism Scale in the 1930s and 1940s, but no remarkable psychometric developments occurred until the introduction of the Belief in Communism Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(McFarland, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: However, the theoretical background of the Belief in Communism Scale is based on Allport and Ross' (1967) model for religious orientation, explicitly assuming a controversial analogy between communism and religious thought, and its psychometric properties have not been subjected to proper cross-cultural validation.
Like the ideologies they aim to measure, psychometric scales evolve alongside changing political landscapes, cultural debates, and disciplinary vocabularies.

Tracing the development of left-wing ideology measurement models requires attention not only to what has been measured, but to how it has been measured-what claims have been foregrounded, which themes have receded, and which new currents have emerged.

Through semantic analysis, we mapped the full corpus of scale items into a shared semantic space (Wulff & Mata, 2025), allowing us to track how the language of ideological measurement models has expanded, fragmented, and reorganized over time.
text.formatted: Through semantic analysis, we mapped the full corpus of scale items into a shared semantic space (Wulff & Mata, 2025), allowing us to track how the language of ideological measurement models has expanded, fragmented, and reorganized over time.

text.text: Political orientation was excluded from the semantic analyses because these measures predominantly consist of abstract left-right or liberal-conservative self-placement items rather than substantive ideological statements, making direct item-content comparisons of limited interpretability.

Operational ideology was also excluded from the semantic maps because it encompasses a broad range of issue domains (e.g., gender, redistribution, the environment, and immigration) and therefore overlaps with virtually the entire conceptual space represented in the figures-including it substantially obscured the temporal trajectories of the more clearly delimited ideological domains.

text.text: We then drew random samples of 100 items per cluster for expert review, assessing thematic coherence.
To support this process, we additionally used the LLM, Meta-LLaMA 3.1-70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), as a tool to generate candidate labels based on the same item samples.

text.text: These candidate labels were subsequently reviewed and curated by domain expert criteria.
This approach yielded a set of interpretable thematic groupings which were refined through further expert validation and consolidated into two explicit thematic taxonomies.
Specifically, the feminism taxonomy comprised eight broad themes, including workplace and economic equality, gender roles, structural and systemic critique, and feminist identity and engagement.
Meanwhile, the environmentalism taxonomy comprised seven themes, including relationship with nature, environmental threat, technology and development, and policy and governance.
Tables S3 and S4 provide the complete set of themes, their constituent subthemes, and detailed descriptions of their item content.

text.text: We then reclassified all items in feminism and environmentalism using these taxonomies via zero-shot classification (Wang et al., 2023), operationalized by prompting the same LLM (Meta-LLaMA 3.1-70B) with the expert-curated thematic categories in a classification instruction (see Sections S4 and S5 for details).

text.text: Classification quality was assessed through exhaustive expert review: the 1,482 feminism items and 1,258 environmentalism items were jointly inspected by the two domain experts against the expert-curated taxonomies.
Because this validation was conducted jointly rather than through independent coding, no formal model-expert agreement coefficient was calculated.
These classifications allowed us to trace the relative salience of each theme over time (Figure 8).

text.text: Within feminism, virtually no specific theme appears before the 1980s.

From the mid-1980s through the 1990s, there is a sharp rise of measurement models dominated by themes such as structural and systemic critique, gender roles, stereotypes and norms, political and civic representation, and equality in the workplace and the economy.

These themes decline in the 2000s, as the field shows an increasing focus on feminist identity and engagement with the feminist movement, as well as anti-feminist attitudes, although the latter has been in decline since the late 2000s.
The theme of reproductive rights and sexual autonomy is slowly increasing, although it remains less prevalent than the other themes.

Of note, while the anti-feminist theme includes oppositional items (e.g., "feminists should be ashamed of what they have done to society"), some may be reverse-coded pro-feminist items, but this is not always reported explicitly in the articles.
This ambiguity should be considered, and the prevalence of this category interpreted with caution.
Within environmentalism, the themes of environmental threat and human relationship with nature began to dominate the field in the 1990s and remain the most prominent themes.
However, from the 2000s, there is an increase of concerns around technological development, environmentalism as an identity (including activism), and environmental policy and governance.
The least measured themes of environmentalism so far have centered on materialism and consumption, as well as long-term and intergenerational ethics.
This systematic review synthesized the psychometric landscape of left-wing ideology by analyzing 1,899 peer-reviewed articles published between 1930 and 2023.

Drawing from nearly 2.4 million participants across 2,024 original samples, we identified and categorized instruments used to assess eight ideological constructs: political orientation, operational ideology, feminism, environmentalism, egalitarianism, communism, left-wing authoritarianism, and progressivism.
We also conducted supplementary analyses on 437 articles that reanalyzed data from large-scale macro surveys (e.g., GSS, ANES), yielding 568 samples.
These analyses identified measurements targeting six constructs: political orientation, operational ideology, feminism, environmentalism, communism, and egalitarianism.
Our findings reveal notable disparities in measurement practices.

Political orientation was most frequently assessed through single-item scales lacking psychometric depth, while constructs such as left-wing authoritarianism and progressivism have only recently begun to receive psychometric attention.
Although feminism and environmentalism have been extensively studied, there is an increasing trend of using identity-focused approaches rather than theoretically grounded measurement models.

The field appears fragmented, characterized by limited scale validation, heavy reliance on WEIRD samples, and inconsistent reporting of psychometric properties-highlighting the need for more rigorous, theory-driven, and culturally sensitive approaches to the measurement of left-wing ideologies.
These trends reflect a broader tension in psychometrics between ease of measurement and conceptual precision (Ellis & Stimson, 2012; Flake & Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: These trends reflect a broader tension in psychometrics between ease of measurement and conceptual precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ellis & Stimson, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Flake & Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The widespread reliance on diffuse, thematically varied scales-particularly within operational ideology-limits cross-study comparability and theoretical coherence.
The results raise important philosophical and methodological questions.
For instance, to what extent is someone who cares about the environment an environmentalist?
Is selfidentification as a feminist sufficient to infer endorsement of specific feminist conceptions?
Conversely, should individuals who reject such labels but endorse their underlying values still be categorized as feminists or environmentalists?

This conceptual ambiguity reflects the conflation of ideological identification with ideological content, as focusing on self-identification or belongingness rather than ideological commitments potentially undermines construct validity (Ellis & Stimson, 2012).
text.formatted: This conceptual ambiguity reflects the conflation of ideological identification with ideological content, as focusing on self-identification or belongingness rather than ideological commitments potentially undermines construct validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ellis & Stimson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals may self-identify as feminists or environmentalists while holding minimal or even contradictory ideological beliefs, whereas others may avoid these labels yet endorse values consistent with feminist or environmentalist principles (Brick et al., 2017; Elder et al., 2021; Macnaghten & Urry, 1998; McCabe, 2005; Zucker, 2004).

text.text: This issue is relevant given that, in both domains-feminism and environmentalism-we found a growing tendency to measure general identification over assessment of specific ideological commitments.
These conceptual challenges are further complicated by the absence of standardized approaches to measuring operational ideology.
Instruments assessing issue-based left-wing attitudes showed limited consistency in theoretical grounding, structure, and psychometric validation.
These measures often rely on varying numbers of items with unclear construct boundaries.
Some variation in issue content is expected and even necessary, as it reflects differences across sociopolitical contexts and the evolving nature of ideology.
However, this context sensitivity can also complicate construct validity and cross-study comparability when the rationale for item selection is not made explicit.
Therefore, findings based on these measures may appear comparable while in fact capturing somewhat different underlying constructs.
Authors employing these measures should explicitly report the specific issues assessed and their rationale for selection, as well as basic evidence of construct validity and internal consistency.
Operational ideology represents a particularly promising target for further semantic analysis.

The open database generated by this review could be used to examine recurring content and potential latent dimensions across operational-ideology measures, helping to clarify their conceptual structure and inform the development of more theoretically coherent and operationally precise instruments.
We also found substantial variation in how the single-item left-right scale of political orientation is used.
Given its prevalence as the most used instrument, this heterogeneity signals an important methodological inconsistency.

Research suggests that scale format meaningfully affects responses. Kroh (2007) found that 11-point scales yielded higher validity than 10-or 101point formats, showing clearer discrimination among ideological positions. Aybar et al. (2024) demonstrated that modest variations-such as shifting from 0-10 to 1-10 scales, changing the number of labeled points, or altering the direction-can influence response distributions, the proportion of centrists, and the inferred ideological profiles of the population. Yeung and Quek (2024) showed that symbolic associations with labels like "liberal" or "conservative" can bias responses, so redefining or removing these labels can influence self-placement.

text.text: Importantly, such measures must go beyond reverse-coded conservatism scales.
An individual disagreeing with items favoring, for example, traditional marriage or military spending, reveals only a rejection of those positions, not which alternative views they hold.

To meaningfully capture left-wing ideology, research would benefit from including positively worded items reflecting positions salient to specific left-wing movements (e.g., indigenous rights, anti-imperialism), or bipolar scales with clearly defined anchors.
Open-ended follow-ups may also serve to elucidate ideological commitments in regions where empirical research remains scarce.
Our findings also reveal a sampling bias in the literature.
Ninety-two percent of samples were drawn from WEIRD countries, and only 8% of articles used nationally representative samples.
Such biases constrain generalizability and are problematic given the global diversity of left-wing traditions.

Outside WEIRD contexts, left-wing ideologies often integrate populist, nationalist, revolutionary, or religious discourses distinct from WEIRD frameworks (Baranowski et al., 2024; Malka et al., 2019; Panizza & Miorelli, 2009).

text.text: These examples highlight the inadequacy of applying psychometric tools developed in WEIRD contexts to other cultural settings.

Assuming that constructs such as "left wing," "progressivism," or "liberalism" are universal, or that rejecting conservative views implies endorsement of typically WEIRD left-wing ideas, risks conceptual misrepresentation.
Another challenge concerns the overrepresentation of university students from Western contexts.
Compared to non-students, these samples tend to be more socially liberal or left leaning (Pew Research Center, 2016; Simon, 2022; Surridge, 2016).
text.formatted: Compared to non-students, these samples tend to be more socially liberal or left leaning <ref type="bibr">(Pew Research Center, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Simon, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Surridge, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Reliance on student samples then risks inflating estimations of ideological extremity and consistency, potentially overrepresenting certain ideological profiles.
For instance, in our systematic review, nearly 60% of studies on communism/socialism, egalitarianism, and feminism used student samples, and nearly 50% of operational ideology studies did likewise.
Notably, all progressivism studies used student samples-though this should be interpreted cautiously given the recent development of progressivism measures and the small number of studies.
Beyond psychometric and sampling limitations, the content of measurement models-and its evolution-presents a critical and often overlooked challenge.
Psychological scales are not static-nor should they be-as the constructs they measure are embedded in changing sociopolitical contexts.
Over the past century, the content of scales has evolved significantly, reflecting broader transformations in public discourse.
While such adaptability helps maintain relevance, it also risks anchoring measurement models in outdated and uncontextualized assumptions.
The computational techniques reported offer a way to monitor this evolution.
By embedding, mapping, and semantically comparing scale items, researchers can detect conceptual overlap or fragmentation and design instruments that better reflect current societal trends.

More specifically, semantic maps can inform scale construction by delineating the content domains that have historically been represented within a construct, identifying areas that remain comparatively underrepresented, and revealing themes that have disappeared from contemporary measures despite potentially retaining theoretical relevance.

They can also help determine whether an emerging instrument disproportionately captures a narrow domain-for example, ideological self-identification-at the expense of substantive doctrinal beliefs, values, or policy commitments.
This information can guide the selection of a more balanced pool of candidate items covering the intended conceptual domain before conventional psychometric validation begins.
These tools help prevent conceptual drift, enhance cross-study comparability, and support more inclusive scale development by highlighting blind spots or underrepresented themes.

A complementary direction for future research would be to systematically trace how established instruments are modified across studies-for example, through changes in item selection, response formats, wording, or scoring-and examine whether such modifications are associated with differences in reliability, factorial structure, or external associations.

Ultimately, treating ideological constructs as historically contingent and evolving-rather than fixed diagnostic categories-can foster a more reflexive and context-sensitive approach to psychometric scale development.

Our semantic analysis revealed that left-wing ideological scales have not only broadened to encompass a wider range of topics but also undergone substantial shifts in how ideological commitments are represented.
Thematic tracking over time showed significant changes in the measurement of feminism and environmentalism.
Feminism scales initially emphasized issues such as structural critique, gender roles, and workplace equality, but have shifted toward measuring identity and engagement with the feminist movement.

Environmentalism measures have predominantly centered on environmental threats and human-nature relationships, but are increasingly incorporating themes of technological development, environmental identity, activism, policy, and governance.

These findings point to a growing diversification of ideological content, alongside a broader trend toward measuring identity and engagement with political movements rather than specific ideological doctrines.

The semantic proximity analysis (Figure 7) also suggests that progressivism occupies a central position, with substantial semantic similarity with egalitarianism, communism, left-wing authoritarianism, feminism, and environmentalism.

text.text: Nevertheless, we note that this interpretation is speculative and more investigation is needed.
This systematic review has several strengths.
First, it adhered to PRISMA guidelines, ensuring methodological rigor and transparency.
Second, its search strategy imposed no restrictions on publication year, methodology, or sample type, enabling a comprehensive historical analysis.
Third, it encompassed a wide variety of left-wing ideological constructs, providing detailed mapping beyond general labels.
Fourth, the cumulative sample size was substantial, offering robust descriptive insights.
Fifth, data extraction was exhaustive, capturing psychometric details such as factor structures, reliability indices, and item content.
Nonetheless, limitations remain.

Some relevant studies may have been missed if the terminology used in their titles, abstracts, or indexing did not align with the search terms, and the review was restricted to English-language publications.
Although English dominates the international psychological literature, this restriction may have contributed to the observed WEIRD and Anglophone sampling bias.

Additionally, the search terms-though comprehensive-were constrained by dominant terminologies in the literature, potentially underrepresenting constructs such as critical social justice, intersectionality, or critical race theory.
In particular, "egalitarian" was not included as a search term, meaning that studies measuring egalitarianism were retrieved only when they also matched other terms in the search strategy.

A further limitation is that the review was designed to examine the psychometric structure, item content, and reported reliability of measures of left-wing ideology, rather than to systematically assess evidence of convergent, discriminant, predictive, or nomological validity.
Finally, temporal changes in the frequency with which particular constructs or instruments are used do not, by themselves, establish why these changes occurred.

For example, the decline in feminism measures following their late twentieth-century peak could reflect the consolidation or saturation of existing measurement models, shifts in research priorities, or changes in how feminist attitudes are operationalized, rather than a decline in scholarly interest.
These explanations should therefore be regarded as hypotheses requiring further investigation.

text.text: These approaches differ substantially in their conceptualization of left-wing authoritarianism.

Whereas Conway et al.'s measure largely preserves the content and structure of traditional right-wing authoritarianism while reversing its ideological direction, the dimensions proposed by Costello et al. vary in their proximity to conventional definitions of authoritarianism: top-down censorship most directly captures support for coercive restrictions, whereas anti-hierarchical aggression and anti-conventionalism also incorporate broader ideological content characteristic of the contemporary political left.

Importantly, Costello et al.'s scale appears to capture forms of progressive authoritarianism characteristic of contemporary WEIRD ideological contexts, with item content particularly aligned with political debates in English-speaking Western countries, rather than authoritarian attitudes more commonly associated with Marxist-Leninist traditions or revolutionary movements in non-WEIRD contexts.
Figure6illustrates how items of feminism and egalitarianism first sparsely occupy the space, while environmentalism emerges in the mid-1970s before booming in the 2010s.
Items on communism appear in the late 1980s, while progressivism and left-wing authoritarianism only gain traction after 2010.
By 2023, feminism and environmentalism items form the two largest, and historically non-overlapping, regions of the semantic space.

Meanwhile, constructs such as communism, egalitarianism, progressivism, and left-wing authoritarianism span a central semantic corridor that links, and in some places overlaps with, the feminism and environmentalism regions.

Figure6.
Cumulative visualization of psychological measurement items used to assess ideology.

Each panel shows the progressive accumulation of items over time, color-coded by ideological theme: communism (blue), egalitarianism (orange), environmentalism (green), feminism (purple), left-wing authoritarianism (red), and progressivism (yellow).
The increasing density and diversity of items reflect the expanding scope of ideological constructs in psychological research.

Feminism and egalitarianism were among the earliest themes to appear, while environmentalism emerged in the mid-1970s and communism in the late 1980s, followed by progressivism and leftwing authoritarianism in the 2010s.

Notably, feminism and environmentalism tend to occupy distinct semantic regions, with limited overlap, whereas communism, egalitarianism, progressivism, and left-wing authoritarianism occupy more central regions of the semantic space.
A more detailed view can be found in FigureS4.2023 was represented by a single advance-published article measuring feminism.
FigureS8for a heatmap depicting pairwise semantic similarity among ideological categories).
Figure7.
Semantic-similarity network of ideological categories.
Each node represents one of six categories-feminism, egalitarianism, progressivism, communism, left-wing authoritarianism, and environmentalism-colored distinctly.
Edges connect each pair of categories based on their mean cosine similarity, computed across all item embeddings within each pair.
Both line thickness and grayscale intensity scale with similarity strength.

text.text: Figure8.
Temporal distribution of articles containing at least one item associated with each thematic category, for feminism (top) and environmentalism (bottom).

In feminism, dominant themes in the late 20th century include structural and systemic critique, gender roles, stereotypes and norms, political and civic representation, and workplace and economic equality, followed by a shift toward more individualized frames such as feminist identity and reproductive rights and sexual autonomy.
In environmentalism, early emphasis on environmental threat and human-nature relationships is later complemented by increased attention to identity and engagement, technology, and governance.

Themes related to consumption and intergenerational ethics have remained less frequently represented in measurement models of environmentalism. 2023 was represented by a single advance-published article measuring feminism.
systematic review provides the first comprehensive synthesis of the psychometric landscape of left-wing ideological measurement in psychology.

By mapping instruments used across nearly a century of research, it highlights the conceptual and methodological fragmentation of the field, the persistent reliance on single-item measures, and the lack of theoretical grounding and validation in multi-item scales.
At the same time, it reveals promising recent efforts to develop psychometric models of left-wing authoritarianism and progressivism.
The findings highlight the need for multidimensional, theory-driven, and culturally sensitive instruments that capture the diversity of left-wing ideological commitments beyond general labels.

Future research would benefit from integrating rigorous psychometric standards with interdisciplinary theoretical frameworks to develop instruments that not only improve measurement precision but also reflect the complex realities of left-wing ideologies in diverse sociopolitical contexts.

The database generated by this review also provides a foundation for future meta-analytic work, including analyses of associations among left-wing ideological constructs, as well as tests of whether such associations vary according to the instruments and measurement approaches employed or across cultural and sociopolitical contexts.

Such advances are essential for moving beyond reductive operationalizations of political ideology toward a nuanced understanding of the psychological and ideological foundations of the political left.
